_note: References the case files cite by id. Metadata (authors, title, journal, year, PMID, DOI) checked against PubMed on the date in metadata_checked. content_check says who has confirmed that a case's use of the source matches what it recommends: every case is clinically reviewed by the owner before it enters an evaluation build.

idsa-uti-2011.authors: Gupta K, Hooton TM, Naber KG, et al.
idsa-uti-2011.title: International clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women: a 2010 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the European Society for Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
idsa-uti-2011.note: Superseded for pyelonephritis by the 2025 cUTI series, which classifies pyelonephritis as complicated; still IDSA's guideline for uncomplicated cystitis. No case cites it since 2026-11-12.

idsa-cuti-2025.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines by Infectious Diseases Society of America: 2025 Guideline on Management and Treatment of Complicated Urinary Tract Infections-Selection of Antibiotic Therapy for Complicated Urinary Tract Infections
idsa-cuti-2025.note: Part of the 2025 cUTI series (with idsa-cuti-2025-ivpo and idsa-cuti-2025-duration). Checked 2026-11-12 against IDSA's published PDF on idsociety.org; owner approved. Oral agents: fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX preferred; oral third-generation cephalosporins may be comparable; cephalexin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and low-bioavailability cephalosporins such as cefdinir to be used cautiously and with optimized dosing. Correction: #123 recorded an earlier confirmation that rested on secondary summaries.

idsa-cuti-2025-ivpo.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines by Infectious Diseases Society of America: 2025 Guidelines on Management and Treatment of Complicated Urinary Tract Infections - Timing of Intravenous to Oral Antibiotics Transition for Complicated Urinary Tract Infections
idsa-cuti-2025-ivpo.note: Checked 2026-11-12 against IDSA's published PDF on idsociety.org; owner approved. Recommendation I: switch to oral therapy in complicated UTI including acute pyelonephritis when clinically improving, able to take oral medication and an effective oral option is available (conditional, low certainty); supporting trials mostly enrolled patients who were afebrile, hemodynamically stable and had source control. After improvement on ceftriaxone, an oral third-generation cephalosporin is a reasonable choice.

idsa-cuti-2025-duration.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines by Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA): 2025 Guidelines on Management and Treatment of Complicated Urinary Tract Infections--Duration of Antibiotics for Complicated UTI
idsa-cuti-2025-duration.note: Checked 2026-11-12 against IDSA's published PDF on idsociety.org; owner approved. 5-7 days of a fluoroquinolone (conditional, moderate certainty) or 7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone (conditional, very low certainty) rather than 10-14 days, from the first day of effective therapy; no longer course for oral beta-lactams, though higher doses may be required; 10-14 days only for men with suspected prostatitis.

fda-cefpodoxime-label.authors: US Food and Drug Administration (manufacturer labeling)
fda-cefpodoxime-label.title: Cefpodoxime proxetil tablets, film coated: prescribing information
fda-cefpodoxime-label.note: Checked 2026-11-12 against the DailyMed label; owner approved: urinary indication is uncomplicated UTI (cystitis) only, 100 mg every 12 hours for 7 days; creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min every 24 hours; on hemodialysis 3 times a week after dialysis; food increases absorption; high-dose antacids or H2 blockers reduce it.

idsa-amr-gn-2024.authors: Tamma PD, Heil EL, Justo JA, et al.
idsa-amr-gn-2024.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America 2024 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections
idsa-amr-gn-2024.note: Superseded by the 2026 guidance (idsa-amr-gn-2026); cases citing it need the owner to confirm the recommendation is unchanged.

idsa-amr-gn-2026.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America 2026 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections
idsa-amr-gn-2026.note: Newer than the drafting agent's knowledge. 2026-11-12 (M6): the AmpC and ESBL changes were checked against IDSA's published 2026 text and approved by the owner: Hafnia alvei added as moderate AmpC risk; completing an empirically started ceftriaxone course may be reasonable in a non-severe infection with clinical improvement and source control (non-severe is not defined); presumed ESBL at a ceftriaxone MIC of 4 ug/mL or more; piperacillin-tazobactam an alternative for ESBL complicated UTI. Its uncomplicated cystitis wording is not yet checked.

idsa-shea-asp-2016.authors: Barlam TF, Cosgrove SE, Abbo LM, et al.
idsa-shea-asp-2016.title: Implementing an Antibiotic Stewardship Program: Guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America

clsi-m100.title: Performance Standards for Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (M100)
clsi-m100.source: CLSI M100, 36th ed. (2026), breakpoint tables for Enterobacterales and Staphylococcus
clsi-m100.note: A standard, not a journal article. The 36th edition (January 2026) is current and FDA-recognized; the breakpoints the cases use have not been rechecked against it.

idsa-meningitis-2004.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
idsa-meningitis-2004.title: Practice guidelines for the management of bacterial meningitis
idsa-meningitis-2004.note: Table 4 (empiric therapy by age and predisposing condition) has no immunocompromised row, so the Listeria rule cites it for the age criterion only. Per OpenEvidence 2026-11-12; the table is an image and was not read here.

escmid-meningitis-2016.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dzupova O, et al.
escmid-meningitis-2016.title: ESCMID guideline: diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis
escmid-meningitis-2016.note: WHO 2025 (who-meningitis-2025) is newer; IDSA 2004 and ESCMID 2016 remain the current society guidelines. Table 4.1 pairs cefotaxime or ceftriaxone with amoxicillin for adults over 50 and for adults with Listeria risk factors (footnote: diabetes mellitus, immunosuppressive drugs, cancer, other immunocompromising conditions); per OpenEvidence 2026-11-12, the publisher page refused automated access and the table was not read here.

who-meningitis-2025.title: WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care
who-meningitis-2025.note: Not indexed in PubMed. Checked 2026-11-12 against the WHO document; owner approved: add ampicillin or amoxicillin to the initial empiric regimen with any Listeria risk factor: age over 60 years, pregnancy, immunosuppressive therapy, organ transplantation, malignancy, advanced HIV disease, diabetes mellitus, end-stage kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, alcohol use disease. Its age threshold (60) is higher than IDSA 2004 and ESCMID 2016 (50); the rule keeps 50 and cites WHO only above 60.

idsa-crbsi-2009.authors: Mermel LA, Allon M, Bouza E, et al.
idsa-crbsi-2009.title: Clinical practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of intravascular catheter-related infection: 2009 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America

idsa-escmid-sab-2026.authors: Infectious Diseases Society of America; European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
idsa-escmid-sab-2026.title: IDSA/ESCMID 2026 Consensus Statements on Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia: Risk Stratification, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Management of Adults and Children
idsa-escmid-sab-2026.note: Not yet in PubMed; update the source when it is. Checked 2026-11-12 on IDSA's page: initial evaluation includes follow-up blood cultures and transthoracic echocardiography; Consensus Statement 4: TEE may be unnecessary in adults with a negative good-quality TTE and no endocarditis increased-risk features. Management of MSSA and MRSA bacteremia is a future part.

idsa-ciai-2010.authors: Solomkin JS, Mazuski JE, Bradley JS, et al.
idsa-ciai-2010.title: Diagnosis and management of complicated intra-abdominal infection in adults and children: guidelines by the Surgical Infection Society and the Infectious Diseases Society of America
idsa-ciai-2010.note: The 2024 IDSA update (Bonomo RA et al., PMID 38965057 and companions) covers risk assessment, imaging and microbiology, not antibiotic selection.

sis-iai-2024.authors: Huston JM, Barie PS, Dellinger EP, et al.
sis-iai-2024.title: The Surgical Infection Society Guidelines on the Management of Intra-Abdominal Infection: 2024 Update
sis-iai-2024.note: Metadata checked; the text is not yet read. Its abstract confirms recommendations on duration. Per a secondary summary, its new 4-day recommendations cover specific groups (percutaneous source control, sepsis, higher-risk patients) and 8 days for the critically ill; confirm that it carries forward the general 4-day course after adequate source control (STOP-IT) before a case relies on it.

ats-idsa-cap-2019.authors: Metlay JP, Waterer GW, Long AC, et al.
ats-idsa-cap-2019.title: Diagnosis and treatment of adults with community-acquired pneumonia. An official clinical practice guideline of the American Thoracic Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America
ats-idsa-cap-2019.source: Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2019;200(7):e45-e67

ats-cap-2025.authors: Jones BE, Ramirez JA, Oren E, et al.
ats-cap-2025.title: Diagnosis and Management of Community-acquired Pneumonia: An Official American Thoracic Society Clinical Practice Guideline
ats-cap-2025.source: Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2026;212(1):24-44
ats-cap-2025.note: Updates four questions of the 2019 guideline, including antibiotic duration; ats-idsa-cap-2019 remains the reference for antibiotic choice. IDSA did not endorse this update (it disagreed on two antibiotic-choice questions). Duration as reported in summaries, owner approved for the duration rule 2026-11-12; the guideline's own text is not yet checked: fewer than 5 days (minimum 3) once clinically stable in nonsevere CAP (conditional, low quality); 5 days or more in severe CAP.
